We have seen your numbers. Now I would like to hear about you. How would your last team describe you?
Approachable, I think, and on top of the detail. But I would rather you heard it from them, so I am happy to give you two names.
Some finance leaders micromanage. Would they say that about you?
They would have, ten years ago. I checked every line of the close myself. These days I would rather give my team the problem than the answer.
And when somebody on your team disagrees with you?
I want to hear it before the decision, not after. My controller was my sounding board for every big call, and she disagreed with me often.
Our culture is very collaborative. Decisions here can take time.
Then we had better agree early on which decisions are mine and which are shared. That saves time for everybody.

We had better agree early on which decisions are mine and which are shared.

When I ask a finance candidate about culture, I am not looking for the right adjectives. Everybody is collaborative and everybody has an open door. What I listen for is one real moment. A time somebody on his team disagreed with him, and what he did the next morning. The strong candidates give me that moment in under a minute, and they tell it with the other person in the story, not only themselves. The weak ones give me a list of values. And the ones I remember are the ones who say what they would rather do, and why, without pretending there is only one way to lead.

I spent fourteen years as a finance director before I started coaching, and the culture question was the one I prepared least. That was a mistake. In a final round, the numbers have already been checked. What is left is whether people want to work with you on a bad Tuesday. My advice now is simple. Pick one habit that shows how you lead, and tell it with a name and a date. If you have changed, say so. I used to check every line myself, and these days I would rather give my team the problem than the answer. That sentence does more in a culture interview than any list of values.

Laura asks how his last team would describe him. He gives two adjectives and offers two names to call. She asks whether finance leaders micromanage, and he says what he used to do and what he does now. She says decisions take time there. He suggests they agree early on which decisions are his.
